extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining whether a claimed invention satisfies the utility requirement of 35 U.S.C. 101 (and the related how-to/use elements of 35 U.S.C. 112) including specific, substantial, and credible utility, therapeutic utilities, inoperativeness, and procedural handling of rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement under 35 U.S.C. 101
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office must examine each application to ensure compliance with the 'useful invention' or utility requirement of 35 U.S.C. 101; to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101 an applicant must claim statutory subject matter and show the claimed invention is 'useful' for some purpose either explicitly or implicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must keep in mind general principles controlling application of the utility requirement, including that utility ensures patents are granted only on inventions that are 'useful.' Application of this element is the focus of the guidelines. The examiner should determine whether the asserted utility is specific, substantial, and credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to and withdrawing utility rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must recognize, fully consider and respond to each substantive element of any response to a rejection based on lack of utility; only where the totality of the record continues to show the asserted utility is not specific, substantial, and credible should a rejection be maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant satisfactorily rebuts a prima facie rejection based on lack of utility under 35 U.S.C. 101, withdraw the 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection and the corresponding rejection imposed under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. Ensure each substantive element of the applicant's response is addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific utility
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'specific utility' is a use for or application of the invention that is specific to the subject matter claimed and can 'provide a well-defined and particular benefit to the public.' General statements (e.g., 'useful biological properties,' 'gene probe' without a target) are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statement of specific utility should fully and clearly explain why the applicant asserts the invention is useful and enable one of ordinary skill in the art to understand the asserted use (for example, explain the purpose or how the invention may be used). Distinguish specific use from broad/general utility; examples (In re Fisher, In re Kirk) illustrate insufficiency when no particular target or application is identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial utility
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'substantial' utility must show an immediate, well-defined, real-world benefit to the public; utilities that require or constitute carrying out further research to identify or reasonably confirm real-world context are not substantial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept any reasonable use identified that provides a public benefit as sufficient for 'substantial' utility. Utilities that do not qualify include: (A) basic research into properties/mechanisms; (B) method of treating an unspecified disease/condition; (C) an assay identifying a material that itself lacks specific/substantial utility; (D) a method of making a material that itself lacks specific/substantial/credible utility; (E) a claim to an intermediate product used to make a final product that lacks specific/substantial/credible utility. Do not interpret 'immediate benefit' to require products/services to be currently available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research tools may qualify as specific and substantial utilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions intended for research or laboratory settings (e.g., gas chromatographs, screening assays, nucleotide sequencing techniques) can have clear, specific and substantial utility and therefore meet the patent utility requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat the label 'research tool', 'intermediate', or 'for research purposes' as dispositive. Distinguish between inventions whose asserted utility is specific and substantial and inventions whose asserted utility requires further research to confirm. Evaluate whether the asserted utility is immediate and well-defined in the context disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperative or 'incredible' utility (total incapacity test)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention that is wholly inoperative (i.e., totally incapable of achieving a useful result) is not 'useful' under patent law; however partial success is sufficient—total incapacity must be shown to sustain a 101 rejection on inoperativeness grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections on inoperativeness are rare and fact-specific. Examples of inventions found inoperative include perpetual motion machines, claims inconsistent with known science, or claims that cannot possibly produce the asserted results. Office personnel should not label an asserted utility 'incredible' or 'speculative' unless it is clear that the invention cannot work as claimed based on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutic and pharmacological utility standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Therapeutic/pharmacological inventions are subject to the same legal utility requirements as other fields: identification of pharmacological activity or a method of treating a particular disorder can satisfy the utility requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of pharmacological activity is beneficial to the public and can constitute practical utility (Nelson v. Bowler). In vitro data, under appropriate circumstances, can establish practical utility by showing pharmacological activity and marshaling further research. FDA approval or Phase II clinical data are not required to satisfy patent utility; do not conflate patent utility with regulatory safety/effectiveness standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 112 first paragraph) and 35 U.S.C. 101
rubrics_metrics.description: A deficiency under the utility prong of 35 U.S.C. 101 also creates a deficiency under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (the 'how to use' and enablement aspects); 112 presupposes compliance with 101 because 'how to use' requires that the invention be useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection for lack of utility is proper, a corresponding 35 U.S.C. 112(a) rejection based on lack of enablement/ability to use should be imposed separately and incorporate by reference the factual basis and conclusions of the 101 rejection. Do not impose a 112(a) lack-of-utility rejection unless there is an appropriate factual basis establishing the 101 deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the claimed invention (claim-by-claim evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must be evaluated on its own merits for compliance with statutory requirements; the claimed invention is the focus of the utility assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally a dependent claim has utility if the independent claim from which it depends has utility and is in the same statutory class. Exception: where the dependent claim specifies a different utility than the independent claim. For genus claims where species within the genus may lack utility, a generic claim should be treated as sufficient unless it can be established that other species clearly encompassed by the claim do not have utility — in such cases encourage amendment to exclude species that lack utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: One credible assertion of specific utility is sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant need only make one credible assertion of specific utility for a claimed invention to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112; additional statements of utility, even if not credible, do not render the claimed invention lacking in utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g., Raytheon v. Roper, In re Gottlieb) supports that meeting at least one stated objective establishes utility. Thus do not reject claims merely because some asserted utilities are speculative if at least one credible utility is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant statements are not alone sufficient basis for a lack-of-utility rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements made by the applicant in the specification or during prosecution cannot, standing alone, be the basis for a lack of utility rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 or 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may include nonessential statements of uncertain technical accuracy; the Office should not require striking such statements. Examiners should avoid reading unclaimed results, limitations, or embodiments into claims, which can inappropriately change the relationship of asserted utility to the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural examination step: determine whether an asserted or well-established utility exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon initial examination the examiner should review the specification to determine if there are any statements asserting that the claimed invention is useful for any particular purpose; a complete disclosure should identify a specific and substantial utility for the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statement of specific and substantial utility should fully and clearly explain why the applicant asserts the invention is useful (i.e., purpose and how it may be used) and must enable one ordinarily skilled in the art to understand why the claimed invention is useful. Examiners should look for such enabling assertions in the specification at the outset of examination.
